title: In One Year, Junk Food Was Eradicated From Mexico’s Schools
author: Fernando Camacho and Enrique Méndez
content:
_This article by[Fernando Camacho and Enrique
Méndez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Fernando%20Camacho%20y%20Enrique%20M%C3%A9ndez)
originally appeared in the [October 29, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/29/sociedad/en-un-ano-se-
erradico-la-comida-chatarra-de-las-escuelas-celebra-mario-delgado), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. The head of the Ministry of Public Education (SEP), Mario
Delgado Carrillo, stated that in a single year junk food was “expelled” from
elementary and middle schools, and said that “we will continue fighting the
big corporations in court so that these products do not return” to the
classrooms.

During his appearance before the Education Committee of the Chamber of
Deputies, as part of the review of President Claudia Sheinbaum’s second State
of the Nation Report, Delgado stressed that, even though “it seemed impossible
to get junk food out of the schools,” it has now been achieved.

Although 139 _amparo_ lawsuits were filed “by the big transnationals, we are
not going to allow those products to return. **We have not lost a single
amparo** , and we have three favorable rulings in the (Supreme) Court that
will allow all the other lawsuits to be resolved in our favor,” Delgado
assured.

According to the secretary, the change was based on the fact that the La
Escuela es Nuestra (The School Is Ours) program “has as its guiding axes the
textbooks that explain how to have a healthy life, which foods support
development, and the importance of physical activity. That is why the
cooperatives have healthy food options.”

In the Green Room of San Lázaro, Delgado also faced multiple criticisms from
opposition deputies, who reproached him for the “failure” of La Escuela es
Nuestra, as well as the results of Mexican students on the PISA test, and even
the “indoctrination” in the content of the free textbooks.

### Limit on the Use of Cell Phones

During his presentation, the official stressed that under the Morena
governments “the trap of closing doors on young people and then shifting the
blame onto them and calling them _ninis_ (neither studying nor working) is
over. Today they are supported with scholarships, dignified schools, and more
places to study, with cutting-edge and relevant degree programs, with health
and socio-emotional education.”

Likewise, he highlighted that “for the first time in the history of Mexico,
all students in public elementary, middle, and high schools arrive at school
with a scholarship under their arm,” so that, by the end of 2026, **22 million
students at all levels will receive financial support**.

He also defended the La Escuela es Nuestra model, which “has served more than
73,000 schools” and has been extended to upper secondary schools. “We have now
served all the public high schools in Mexico, benefiting a total of 8.8
million students in elementary, middle, and high schools,” he said.

In the same vein, he added that “more than 154 million free textbooks arrived
at the schools on time,” and highlighted that on November 3 a “unanimous
agreement” will take effect throughout the national education system to
**limit the use of cell phones and mobile devices** in schools at all levels.

Delgado highlighted the Sheinbaum government’s goal of reaching 400,000 new
high school places by 2030, to achieve a gross enrollment rate of more than 90
percent, which he described as “unprecedented,” as well as the elimination of
the exam of the Metropolitan Commission of Public Institutions of Upper
Secondary Education (Comipems).

Regarding teachers’ salary conditions, he emphasized that “in 2026, 200,000
permanent positions have been granted, adding up to a total of 1.2 million
since 2018. Last year the salary increased 10 percent and this year 9 percent,
a recovery in real terms of 80 percent since 2018.”

### “We Don’t Want Show-Offs Who Farm Aura”: PAN

One of the legislators who most forcefully challenged Delgado’s performance
was PAN member Laura Cristina Márquez, who warned of a probable “historic
dropout” of 63,000 children at the elementary level and almost 640,000 young
people in high school, and also reproached Delgado for not referring to the
deficiencies in students’ learning and the cuts in funds for teacher training
and retirees’ pensions.

The legislator asked him why the number of schools with poor infrastructure
conditions supposedly has increased from 37 to 50 percent from 2022 to 2025,
as well as about the causes of Mexico’s low results on the PISA test,
especially in mathematics, reading comprehension, and science.

Likewise, she questioned “why he keeps (free) textbooks full of errors and
loaded with ideology” and “why he allows the promotion of the culture of
hatred and death.” Now on a roll, she told him that “families do not want
empty promises, nor acrobatic speeches, nor show-offs who farm aura,” in
reference to a video posted on the TikTok platform by the head of the SEP last
August, in which he joined that youth trend.

Her fellow party member Liliana Ortiz Pérez also alluded to the video and
complained to Delgado: “we want seriousness for all students, and it is not
worthy of you to play with it. Good education is not farmed on TikTok: it is
built in the classrooms and demonstrated with results.”

After warning about the increase in acts of violence in schools, the PAN
deputy did not let go of the reference: “we don’t need your TikToks, but
schools where students are protected. If you want to talk about aura, worry
about restoring electricity to all the schools in Mexico.”

For her part, Xitlalic Ceja (PRI) indicated that under the Morena governments
“education has been transformed into indoctrination” and questioned him: “if
public education is so good, where do the children and grandchildren of the
elite that governs the country today study? Why do they study in very
expensive schools that millions of Mexicans cannot afford?”

Ignoring the calls from the secretary of the Committee, María Luisa Mendoza
(PVEM), to end her remarks, having used up the three minutes agreed for all
legislators, the PRI member repeated up to three times (amid shouts of protest
from the majority bloc) that student scholarships must not be conditioned “in
exchange for spurious votes and false promises.”

After the umpteenth request to finish speaking, and while Ceja lamented the
“abandonment of teachers,” Mendoza ordered the audio of the microphone that
the PRI deputy was still using to be cut off.

### “They Get a Little Angry About the Scholarships”: Delgado

In response to the opposition’s criticisms, Delgado Carrillo said in a mocking
tone that “some keep grumbling and get a little angry” because students at all
educational levels receive financial support, reaching 22 million scholarship
recipients in 2026, with an investment of 136 billion pesos.

In that regard, he stated that “before, young people became hitmen, but we
turn them into scholarship holders. We are not the same (as the PRI and PAN);
we do not give scholarships for electoral reasons,” and asserted that the
school dropout rate last year was **9.3 percent, down from 14 percent in
2017**.

Faced with complaints about the supposed “indoctrination” in the free
textbooks, he retorted:

> If giving them a framework of critical thinking is indoctrination, accuse us
> of indoctrination. If educating for freedom is indoctrination, accuse us of
> indoctrinating an entire generation to be free in a sovereign Mexico.
>
> Mario Delgado, Secretary of Public Education
